Low Cost Lessons for SAA

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SAA has embarked on yet another cost-cutting exercise designed to return the airline to profit, but is it an old fashioned solution to a modern problem?

Unique Selling Point:
Is cutting costs, aircraft and routes the secret to turning around an ailing, bail-out dependent airline? Efficiency is certainly one ingredient in the profitability recipe, but there are suggestions that SAA's backwardness is what's cooking its goose. And, we're going to fly from Dublin to Prague for less than a 1000 bucks to show you why.

Summary:
In explaining the national carrier's latest bid for a government guarantee, SAA's executive pointed out that unprofitable routes, inefficient planes and a bloated staff were among the reasons for its financial woes. The answer, apparently, would be to reduce the number of aircraft, cut unprofitable routes and limit frequency. In other words, downsize your way to profitability and, in the process, inconvenience your customer while providing a gap to your competitors.

The question is: why does SAA find it so hard to make a profit on even the busiest of routes when other airlines, like Kulula locally and Ethiopian internationally are almost always in the black? That question becomes even more bothersome when you consider that you can fly from Jo'burg to Cape Town on Kulula for R900 return and from Jo'burg to Dublin on Ethiopian for R7000 - both substantially cheaper than SAA.

Perhaps the lesson lies not in rampant downsizing, but in being more innovative. Why, in 2018 does SAA still serve meals on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, does SAA still have business class seats on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, are you unable to pre-pay for an economy class seat in a more comfortable part of the cabin on long-haul flights?

These are some of the low cost innovations that other airlines have embraced. Each has the potential to add to the bottom line, and create an opportunity for growth rather than cuts.

Further information:
This insert will examine the low cost flight model - offering the basics for free, but charging for everything else - and its lessons for the SAA turnaround. It will include a video diary of a flight from Dublin to Europe at very low cost, as well as interviews with the CEO of Kulula, an other at SAA and various industry experts in SA and Europe.

Press Release:


With billions of rands in debt and mounting calls for the airline to shut its doors, the national carrier South African Airways, is in big trouble. SAA's executives say that unprofitable routes, inefficient planes and a bloated staff compliment are among the reasons for its financial woes. Now the state-owned carrier is on the hunt for an equity partner to acquire a stake in the airline. As SAA continues with yet another cost-cutting exercise designed to return the entity to profitability, Carte Blanche explores international low cost models that could provide the answers.

Script:


Script: SAA v Low Cost.

VO: Running an airline is about numbers. It’s a battle of attrition fought in the pages of income statements and balance sheets; where victory or defeat are determined by which figures you have in what column. It’s a battle South African Airways has been losing for some time. (16 sec)

ITV Leon Louw (01:17:44:06) It is now a farce, a joke. It’s a sick joke, a perverse joke, a joke that plunders the poor.

ITV Linden Birns (07:23:22:15) To an extent they have inherited a shopping trolley with the wheels all pointing in different directions and they are trying to get it in line and going point where they want to go.

VO: And there’s mounting frustration among the airline’s critics. (3 sec)

ITV: Leon Louw (01:07:07.07) to keep it going as this embarrassing apartheid dinosaur that has long outlived any useful function and is no longer how airlines are run in the world.

Link: If you were to equate the financial crisis at SAA with an area of turbulence, it would be the type of shaking and banging that has half the passengers checking for the nearest emergency exit and the other half reaching for their sick bags – it really is that dire: billions of Rands of debt and billions of Rands of ongoing losses.

VO: In fact, dire might be an understatement. Accounting is a complicated business, but here are the headlines:
* SAA lost 1.84 billion in the final three months of the last financial year
* Its losses for that entire period - 5.67 billion.
* And it’s got existing debt of 9.2 billion

In the past, government has had to stump up the cash to keep SAA in the air, and, over the next three years, will again have to contribute to the 21.7 billion rand the airline says it needs to keep going.
Why 3 years? Well, that’s how long the new CEO, Vuyani Jarana has given himself to put SAA back on course and return it to profit. (45 sec)

ITV Vuyani Jarana (01:45:13:08) We do know that we are at the point where we have to really start looking at ourselves and making hard decisions.

VO: Hard decisions, he says, are based on the belief that this is an airline that can be saved. And that’s exactly the message presented to SAA’s only current shareholder – the government. (12 sec)

ITV Vuyani Jarana (02:26:04:09) Our sense and my sense actually is that the airline is salvageable and that’s why we presented to the shareholders a strategic recovery plan but we gave the shareholder all options and said look these are the scenarios but we believe the best plan for you is the strategic recovery which is the path we have taken.

VO: Vocal SAA critic and Executive Director of the Free Market Foundation, Leon Louw, believes - as was the case with previous turn-arounds - that decision is going to cost. (12 sec)

ITV Leon Louw (01:04:01:04) You see all the money it gets, all of the so called turn around, bail outs, guarantees, different names for really the same thing which is money being thrown down the bottomless pit.

VO: However, despite the enormous sums involved there is another view. (5 sec)

ITV Linden Birns (07:17:07:14) To be fair to SAA, this is something they have been raising the flag on now for nearly a quarter of a century. Back already in the 90's, they were saying we are not adequately capitalized for what we need to do. We need to be on a firm solid foundation before we can go forwards.

VO: In other words, according to airline industry expert, Linden Birns, while lots of money has come from government it’s never quite been enough. And, that’s led to the latest in a series of turn-around plans that can best be described in three words: cut, cut and cut. Cut jobs, cut aircraft, cut routes and cut costs. (20 sec)

ITV Linden Birns: So now we have got this deferred turn around and unfortunately requires an aggressive intervention and as the CEO himself is saying, using the language of prune to grow, its amputation time.

ITV Vuyani Jarana (01:51:26:16) I refer to it as almost like 'fit for growth' plan if you like. So we have to strengthen the muscle so that we can be fit to compete in the market.

Link: The theory behind prune to grow is exactly as the name suggests: cutting back some of the excess foliage to create an environment for future growth. The danger, of course, is that, if you trim too much, what you’re left with is, well, a little worthless.

VO: In other words, you could cut yourself into oblivion. (4 sec)
ITV Vuyani Jarana (01:53:01:20) That is always the risk, that is why it has to be well thought through. You have to understand what are the areas where you have got, you've got excess fat.

VO: Time, though, is not on Jarana’s side. While those areas of excess fat are identified, the losses are stacking up. (8 sec)

Link: So, while SAA continues to flush away the cash there are airlines around the world that are able to run efficiently and make money. And, increasingly, they’re the so-called low- cost airlines.

Travel Diary.
VO: It’s early on a weekday morning, and in a while I’ll be catching a short international flight. (5 sec)

(PAUSE) I’ll be travelling from the Irish capital, Dublin, to London, England. (5 sec)

(PAUSE) It’s a round trip of about 970kms and it cost me the grand sum of around R630 - that’s R315 each way. Too cheap to be profitable, surely? (12 sec)

On-line booking

VO: Well, not in the domain of a seemingly successful Low-Cost-Carrier like Ryanair. When it comes to making money, few do it better. Its online platform is designed to extract as much cash as possible from its passengers. Anything from seats, to checked bags, additional bags, and the chance to be one of the first onto the plane is up for sale.
Ryanair made an after-tax profit of about R20 billion last year. (28 Sec)

But, the European market is very different to our own, so how do this country’s low-cost carriers compare? Well, on price, very favourably. (9 Sec)

Kulula online booking
A return journey of roughly the same distance and duration on Kulula – say from Durban to Johannesburg at the end of this month – will cost less than R800 for the base-line fare. What’s more, unlike with Ryanair, you get to put a bag in the hold free of charge. (17 Sec)

ITV: Linden Birns (07:10:11.22) It’s a different thing for a legacy carrier where you have a certain model with certain structured costs and some of those are very difficult to adjust or to bring down without taking very aggressive measures and interventions.

VO: So, as SAA attempts an aggressive turn-around should it be borrowing from the Low-Cost playbook – especially on domestic and regional routes? (8 Sec)
Well. In some ways it already is:

VO: It’s attempting to cut costs by, amongst other measures, reducing routes and the size of its fleet

But, it can’t slash fares until its costs are substantially reduced and, besides, it already has a low-cost subsidiary in the form of Mango Airlines.

And, without cutting fares, there’s a limit to how many extras – like priority boarding and checked bags - its passengers would be prepared to pay for. (29 sec)

SAA online booking
Remember that Kulula flight between Durban and Johannesburg later this month? Well, a booking on SAA on the same day - taking flights at roughly similar times – will set you back more than R2000 for a standard ticket. Now, try charging that and then expecting your passengers to also pay for the snacks they currently get for free.

SAA, though, doesn’t consider Kulula competition, and has no intention of getting into a price war. (26 sec)

ITV Vuyani Jarana (02:01:06:01) we have to very careful that we don’t get dragged into a game where it is a lose/lose game. So, we are clear on market segmentation. (CUT to 02:03:29:04) if I then take a full-service carrier and compete with a low cost, their economics are very different altogether. Therefore, I will never succeed, I will lose.

VO: But if he’s not going to compete with their prices, there are at least two other lessons Jarana has taken from the low-cost model. The need to modernise and innovate. (10 sec)

ITV Vuyani Jarana (02:33:49.01) …we know that we a strong brand, very credible brand in the market, built over many years, but the market has moved, we have to move with it. We have to be competitive. We have to be innovative, we have to put more time on the task to make sure we can do it. We must be agile.

(SCREEN GRABS KLM AND BA)

VO: And being innovative has benefits for long-haul operations too. Dutch airline, KLM, for example, has divided its economy class seating into different sections and at different prices. While British Airways has started selling cheaper economy class fares for people travelling without a suitcase.
And, then there are philosophical lessons, too. (22 sec)

ITV Vuyani Jarana (02:33:49.01) at the end of the day it is about transforming the culture of SAA. We have to create a winning culture. A culture where people stop believing that they are being owed a living by somebody else.

VO: The question, though, remains whether that’s possible in the three years Jarana has set himself. (5 sec)

John Webb Question: Do you think SAA can be turned around?

ITV Linden Birns ([07:25:47.11) I think going in the airlines favour is the fact that the demand for air travel in Africa is growing at a pace that is faster than anywhere else in the world. To build 5 km of runway costs a lot less than 5 km of highway. The highway gets you from a-b, the runway gets you from a to everywhere else in between.

VO: A punch drunk public is likely to remain sceptical. (4 sec)

ITV Leon Louw (01:10:42.02) Mr. Jarana is a very fine business man, a proven business person and I believe that if anyone can save it, he can (CUT)...but if he fails, every reasonable human being needs to say that’s it. This is the end. Close it down, it is finished.

VO: It remains to be seen whether government will be forced to make that call. (5 sec)
Ends..

Dutch airline, KLM, for example, has divided its economy class seating into different sections and at different prices. While British Airways has started selling cheaper economy class fares for people travelling without a suitcase. And, then there are philosophical lessons, too. (22 sec) ITV Vuyani Jarana (02:33:49.01) at the end of the day it is about transforming the culture of SAA. We have to create a winning culture. A culture where people stop believing that they are being owed a living by somebody else. VO: The question, though, remains whether that’s possible in the three years Jarana has set himself. (5 sec) John Webb Question: Do you think SAA can be turned around? ITV Linden Birns ([07:25:47.11) I think going in the airlines favour is the fact that the demand for air travel in Africa is growing at a pace that is faster than anywhere else in the world. To build 5 km of runway costs a lot less than 5 km of highway. The highway gets you from a-b, the runway gets you from a to everywhere else in between. VO: A punch drunk public is likely to remain sceptical. (4 sec) ITV Leon Louw (01:10:42.02) Mr. Jarana is a very fine business man, a proven business person and I believe that if anyone can save it, he can (CUT)...but if he fails, every reasonable human being needs to say that’s it. This is the end. Close it down, it is finished. VO: It remains to be seen whether government will be forced to make that call. (5 sec) Ends..

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): SAA has embarked on yet another cost-cutting exercise designed to return the airline to profit, but is it an old fashioned solution to a modern problem?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Is cutting costs, aircraft and routes the secret to turning around an ailing, bail-out dependent airline? Efficiency is certainly one ingredient in the profitability recipe, but there are suggestions that SAA's backwardness is what's cooking its goose. And, we're going to fly from Dublin to Prague for less than a 1000 bucks to show you why.
metadata.Summary: In explaining the national carrier's latest bid for a government guarantee, SAA's executive pointed out that unprofitable routes, inefficient planes and a bloated staff were among the reasons for its financial woes. The answer, apparently, would be to reduce the number of aircraft, cut unprofitable routes and limit frequency. In other words, downsize your way to profitability and, in the process, inconvenience your customer while providing a gap to your competitors. The question is: why does SAA find it so hard to make a profit on even the busiest of routes when other airlines, like Kulula locally and Ethiopian internationally are almost always in the black? That question becomes even more bothersome when you consider that you can fly from Jo'burg to Cape Town on Kulula for R900 return and from Jo'burg to Dublin on Ethiopian for R7000 - both substantially cheaper than SAA. Perhaps the lesson lies not in rampant downsizing, but in being more innovative. Why, in 2018 does SAA still serve meals on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, does SAA still have business class seats on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, are you unable to pre-pay for an economy class seat in a more comfortable part of the cabin on long-haul flights? These are some of the low cost innovations that other airlines have embraced. Each has the potential to add to the bottom line, and create an opportunity for growth rather than cuts.
metadata.Further information: This insert will examine the low cost flight model - offering the basics for free, but charging for everything else - and its lessons for the SAA turnaround. It will include a video diary of a flight from Dublin to Europe at very low cost, as well as interviews with the CEO of Kulula, an other at SAA and various industry experts in SA and Europe.
